name: I. M. Pei
bio:
I. M. Pei (1917–2019) was a Chinese-American architect known for buildings of strong, simple geometry in concrete, stone and glass. Born in Guangzhou, he studied at MIT and Harvard, founded I. M. Pei & Associates in 1955 (later Pei Cobb Freed & Partners), and won the Pritzker Prize in 1983.

His first major recognition came with the Mesa Laboratory (NCAR) near Boulder, Colorado (1967). For the National Gallery of Art, East Building in Washington (1978), he split an awkward trapezoid site into two triangles: one for the public galleries, one for offices and research. The Louvre Pyramid in Paris (1989), a glass-and-metal entrance 21.6 metres high, brings daylight into a new hall below the courtyard and set off years of public debate. The Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong (1990) carries its weight through triangular frames down to four corner columns. Late in life Pei drew on the Chinese traditions that shaped his youth: the Suzhou Museum (2006) uses sloping roofs, white stucco walls and a garden courtyard. I. M. Pei's projects show students how pure geometry can solve a difficult site.

name: Tadao Ando
bio:
Tadao Ando (born 1941) is a Japanese architect, self-taught and once a boxer, known for smooth cast-in-place concrete, simple geometry and the way he draws light, water and landscape into his buildings. The historian Francesco Dal Co described his work as "critical regionalism", and Ando won the Pritzker Prize in 1995.

His Row House in Sumiyoshi in Osaka (1976) is a small two-storey concrete house with no outside windows, lit instead through a central courtyard crossed by a walkway. The Church of the Light in Ibaraki (1989) lets daylight in through a cross cut into the concrete wall behind the altar, from floor to ceiling and wall to wall. On the island of Naoshima, the Chichu Art Museum (2004) is buried underground yet lights much of its art, including paintings from Monet's Water Lilies series, with daylight alone. The Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth (2002) sets three long pavilions in a reflecting pond. Tadao Ando's projects are studied for how one material, daylight and a careful route through a building can create calm.

name: Santiago Calatrava
bio:
Santiago Calatrava (born 1951) is a Spanish-Swiss architect, structural engineer, sculptor and painter, known for bridges held by a single leaning pylon and for stations, museums and concert halls whose forms often recall living creatures. He studied architecture in Valencia and civil engineering at ETH Zurich, where he earned a doctorate in 1981.

The Alamillo Bridge in Seville (1992), built for Expo 92, hangs its deck from one pylon 142 metres high, leaning at 58 degrees, and made his name. Gare do Oriente in Lisbon (1998), built for that year's World Exposition, raises its platforms 19 metres above the road under a lattice of glass and metal. The Milwaukee Art Museum, Quadracci Pavilion (2001) adds a glass entrance hall to Eero Saarinen's earlier building, with a sun screen of moving steel wings. The Turning Torso in Malmö (2005) was his first skyscraper and the first twisting tower. In Valencia, his City of Arts and Sciences (1998) includes L'Hemisfèric, a half-sunk globe whose screen opens and closes like an eye. Santiago Calatrava's projects are studied for how engineering and sculpture can become one structure.

name: Arata Isozaki
bio:
Arata Isozaki (1931–2022) was a Japanese architect and theorist who refused to keep to one style, treating each design as an answer to its context. As a boy he saw Hiroshima destroyed across the water, and he later said his first experience of architecture was its absence. He trained and worked under Kenzō Tange, opened his own office in 1963, and won the Royal Gold Medal in 1986 and the Pritzker Prize in 2019.

Reyner Banham saw his early work as a mix of New Brutalism and Metabolism, although Isozaki had declined to sign the Metabolist manifesto of 1960. The Gunma Museum of Modern Art (1974) comes from these years. The Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles (1986) became his best-known work in the United States. The Palau Sant Jordi in Barcelona (1990) was a main indoor venue of the 1992 Olympics, and the Team Disney Building in Florida (1991) holds what was then the largest sundial. At the Qatar National Convention Centre in Doha (2011), the front columns stand for the Sidra tree of Islamic tradition. Arata Isozaki's buildings show one architect changing approach from site to site.

name: Frank Lloyd Wright
bio:
Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959) was an American architect, designer and writer who designed more than 1,000 structures over 70 years. He called his approach "organic architecture", design in harmony with people and the land. He pioneered the Prairie School, later developed the Usonian home, and trained hundreds of apprentices in his Taliesin Fellowship. In 2019, eight of his buildings were listed together as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Unity Temple in Oak Park (1908) is built of reinforced concrete, with flat overhanging slabs instead of a spire. The Robie House in Chicago (1910), one of his finest Prairie houses, steps its terraces across several levels under cantilevered roofs. Fallingwater in Pennsylvania stands partly over a waterfall on Bear Run, its terraces cantilevered from a central chimney. In the Johnson Wax Headquarters in Racine (1939), concrete columns topped by wide "calyxes" hold up the great workroom, with windows of Pyrex glass tubes. The Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in New York (1959) wraps its gallery in a six-storey spiral ramp under a central skylight. Frank Lloyd Wright's buildings are studied for how they tie a building to its site.

name: Kengo Kuma
bio:
Kengo Kuma (born 1954) is a Japanese architect and emeritus professor at the University of Tokyo, known for buildings that thin and break up their walls into layers of timber, stone and glass so they feel light. He founded Kengo Kuma & Associates in 1990, and works with Japanese craftsmen in wood, earth and paper, keeping their techniques alive while adapting them to modular building. His book Anti-Object sets out the idea.

The Nakagawa-machi Bato Hiroshige Museum (2000) won the Togo Murano Award. The Japan National Stadium in Tokyo (2019), built for the 2020 Olympics, uses timber as a main part of its structure, sourced from all 47 of Japan's prefectures, in modular pieces that can be replaced as they age. The Asakusa Culture Tourist Information Center in Tokyo (2012) looks like a stack of separate wooden buildings set at different angles, wrapped in cedar louvres. V&A Dundee (2018), his first building in the United Kingdom, was meant as "a living room for the city". Kengo Kuma's projects are studied for how natural materials and layered surfaces can make a large building feel close and soft.

name: Jean Nouvel
bio:
Jean Nouvel (born 1945) is a French architect known for buildings that answer their place and climate with screens, patterns and filtered light. He studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. His Arab World Institute in Paris (1987), whose south wall is made of mechanical lenses, like Arabic latticework, that open and shut with the daylight, brought him international fame, and he won the Pritzker Prize in 2008.

The Musée du quai Branly in Paris (2006) raises its main gallery 10 metres over a garden like a bridge and covers one wall in living plants. Torre Glòries in Barcelona (2005), first called Torre Agbar, was designed to recall a geyser rising into the air and carries 4,500 LED lights on its skin. The Louvre Abu Dhabi (2017) shelters its galleries under a 7,000-tonne dome meant to evoke sunlight falling through palm fronds in an oasis. The National Museum of Qatar in Doha (2019) takes its form from the desert rose crystal: 539 interlocking discs that shade visitors from the heat. Jean Nouvel's projects are studied for how each design is made for one site rather than a house style.

name: Kenzō Tange
bio:
Kenzō Tange (1913–2005) was a Japanese architect and urban planner who joined traditional Japanese building to modernism and became one of the first Japanese architects known around the world. Inspired early by Le Corbusier, he later mentored and championed the Metabolist movement, and he won the Royal Gold Medal in 1965 and the Pritzker Prize in 1987.

His winning design for the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park raised the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum (1955) off the ground on a frame and set it on an axis running through the park. The Kagawa Prefectural Government Office (1958) has been likened to the Daibutsu style of Nara's Tōdai-ji temple, with thin columns that leave room for glass. For the 1964 Tokyo Olympics, the first held in Asia, the Yoyogi National Gymnasium hangs its roof skin from two masts. St. Mary's Cathedral in Tokyo (1964) rises from a cross-shaped plan as eight curved shells clad in stainless steel, opening into a cross of light. The Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (1991) sets two towers over a civic plaza. Kenzō Tange's projects are studied for structure, city planning and the meeting of Japanese tradition and modernism.

name: Toyo Ito
bio:
Toyo Ito (born 1941) is a Japanese architect known for light, open, conceptual buildings that try to express both the physical world and the virtual, information-filled city. Born in Seoul to Japanese parents, he worked for Kiyonori Kikutake before opening his own studio in Tokyo in 1971, and he won the Pritzker Prize in 2013.

His early ideas were tested on small houses such as the Silver Hut (1984), his own home; a Silver Hut now forms part of his architecture museum on Ōmishima island in Imabari. The Sendai Mediatheque (2001) holds a library, a film and media collection and a theatre inside an almost cubic glass box. Its seven floor plates, a honeycomb of steel filled with lightweight concrete, rest on thirteen irregular steel tubes that rise like a forest. The building came through the March 2011 earthquake with little or no damage. The Tama Art University Library in Tokyo (2007) is built from thin arches of steel plate and concrete that span up to 12 metres. Toyo Ito's projects are studied for how a new idea of structure can open up the plan of a building.

name: Philip Johnson
bio:
Philip Johnson (1906–2005) was an American architect and curator whose long career ran from modernism to postmodernism. In 1932 he and Henry-Russell Hitchcock staged the Museum of Modern Art's first exhibition of modern architecture, which gave the International Style its name, and in 1979 he became the first winner of the Pritzker Prize. In the 1930s he openly praised Hitler and the Nazi Party and voiced antisemitic views, which he renounced when the United States entered the Second World War.

His own Glass House in New Canaan, Connecticut (1949), a glass room in the landscape, was openly influenced by Mies van der Rohe's Farnsworth House, and he later worked with Mies on the Seagram Building in New York. From 1967 he worked in partnership with John Burgee. The Crystal Cathedral in Garden Grove, California (1980) wraps a 2,248-seat church in 10,000 panes of reflective glass. The AT&T Building (550 Madison Avenue) in New York (1984), a pink granite tower topped by a broken pediment, became a landmark of postmodernism. Philip Johnson's buildings let students follow the main shifts in 20th-century architecture through the work of one architect.

name: Mies van der Rohe
bio:
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe (1886–1969) was a German-American architect and one of the pioneers of modern architecture, known for buildings of industrial steel and plate glass. He was the last director of the Bauhaus, emigrated to the United States after the Nazis came to power, and led the architecture school at what is now the Illinois Institute of Technology in Chicago. Two sayings are tied to him: "less is more" and "God is in the details".

The Barcelona Pavilion (1929), designed with Lilly Reich for the International Exposition and rebuilt in 1986, sets free-standing walls of marble, onyx and tinted glass on a grid of chrome-clad, cross-shaped steel columns. At Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930), a translucent onyx wall changes in the low evening sun. The Farnsworth House in Plano, Illinois (1951) raises a glass house on eight steel columns above a floodplain. S. R. Crown Hall in Chicago (1956) is an early clear-span building, and the Seagram Building in New York (1958) wraps its tower in glass and bronze behind a public plaza. Mies van der Rohe's buildings are studied for structure, proportion and precise detail.

name: SOM
bio:
SOM (Skidmore, Owings & Merrill) is an American architecture, engineering and urban planning firm founded in Chicago in 1936 by Louis Skidmore and Nathaniel Owings, joined in 1939 by the engineer John O. Merrill. It helped bring modernism to the United States and is known above all for skyscrapers. The firm twice received the AIA Architecture Firm Award, in 1962 and 1996, and its partner Gordon Bunshaft won the Pritzker Prize in 1988.

Lever House in New York (1952), by Gordon Bunshaft and Natalie de Blois, was the city's first International Style office building: a curtain wall of glass and stainless steel on an avenue of masonry. The Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library at Yale in New Haven (1963) has walls of marble only 32 millimetres thick that glow amber in daylight. The Hajj Terminal at King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah (1981) was built for the pilgrimage season alone. The Burj Khalifa in Dubai (2010), the world's tallest building at 828 metres, stands on a buttressed central core and three wings. SOM's projects are studied for how closely its architects and engineers design together.

name: Álvaro Siza
bio:
Álvaro Siza (born 1933) is a Portuguese architect from Matosinhos, near Porto, known for buildings that read and answer their landscape and city. "Architects do not invent anything," he has said, "they transform reality." He graduated from the Porto school of architecture in 1955 and later taught there with Fernando Távora. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1992 and the Venice Biennale's Golden Lion for lifetime achievement in 2012.

Among his earliest works to gain public attention, the Leça Swimming Pools (1966) are tidal pools on the shore at Leça da Palmeira. The Boa Nova Tea House (1963) sits among the rocks, reached by a stepped path that hides and reveals the sea. The Faculty of Architecture, University of Porto (1996) and the Serralves Museum of Contemporary Art (1999) are among his best-known works in Porto. He designed the Portugal Pavilion for Expo '98 in Lisbon, and the Iberê Camargo Foundation in Porto Alegre (2008), his first project in Brazil, won a Golden Lion at the 2002 Venice Biennale. Álvaro Siza's projects are studied for how a building can grow out of its site, light and views.

name: Moshe Safdie
bio:
Moshe Safdie (born 1938) is an architect and urban planner, born in Haifa and a citizen of Canada, Israel and the United States, known for socially responsible design in housing, memorials and large public buildings. His first building, Habitat 67 in Montreal, grew out of his master's thesis at McGill University, and he apprenticed with Louis Kahn. He received the Wolf Prize in Architecture in 2019.

Habitat 67 (1967), built for that year's World's Fair, stacks 354 identical prefabricated concrete units into three pyramids up to 12 storeys high, so that each home has a garden terrace on the roof of the one below. At Yad Vashem in Jerusalem, the Children's Memorial (1987) is a mirrored room that reflects the light of five candles, and the Holocaust History Museum (2005) is a triangular concrete prism cut through the hill and lit by a 200-metre skylight. In Singapore, Marina Bay Sands (2010) joins three hotel towers with a 340-metre SkyPark, and Jewel Changi Airport (2019) surrounds the world's tallest indoor waterfall with a terraced forest. Moshe Safdie's projects are studied for density, landscape and daylight at a large scale.

name: Fumihiko Maki
bio:
Fumihiko Maki (1928–2024) was a Japanese architect whose work often explored new materials and brought together the cultures of East and West. A student of Kenzō Tange at the University of Tokyo and a graduate of Harvard, he taught in the United States and returned to Japan in 1960 to help found the Metabolist group. He won the Pritzker Prize in 1993.

He worked on Hillside Terrace in Tokyo (1992) for almost a quarter of a century from 1967, adding to it piece by piece along one street. Spiral in Tokyo (1985) has a façade of aluminium and glass that reflects the jumbled streets around it. The Tokyo Metropolitan Gymnasium (1990) and Makuhari Messe near Tokyo (1989) are among his large public buildings in Japan. Abroad, he designed 4 World Trade Center in New York (2013) on the rebuilt site, and the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto (2014), made to use natural light and clad in sandblasted white granite that plays sun against deep shadow. Fumihiko Maki's projects are studied for their careful detail and for how a building can join a city over time.

name: Kisho Kurokawa
bio:
Kisho Kurokawa (1934–2007) was a Japanese architect and one of the founders of the Metabolist movement. He studied under Kenzō Tange at the University of Tokyo, and as early as 1958 he predicted a "transition from the Age of the Machine to the Age of Life", returning again and again to ideas of metabolism, recycling, ecology and sustainability.

The Nakagin Capsule Tower in Tokyo's Ginza district (1972) was the world's first example of capsule architecture: prefabricated, replaceable rooms fixed to a core, with the capsules, lifts, pipes and ducts all left exposed. It was demolished in 2022, but 23 capsules were set aside for preservation and reuse. His later work includes museums such as the National Museum of Ethnology in Suita (1977), the Hiroshima City Museum of Contemporary Art (1988) and the National Art Center, Tokyo (2007). Kuala Lumpur International Airport (1998) earned him the Dedalo-Minosse International Prize in 2003 and was the first airport to receive Green Globe 21 certification. Kisho Kurokawa's buildings are studied for the Metabolist idea of architecture that can grow, change and be renewed.

name: Louis Kahn
bio:
Louis Kahn (1901–1974) was an Estonian-born American architect based in Philadelphia, known for monumental buildings that do not hide their weight, their materials or the way they are put together. He worked mostly in textured brick and bare concrete set against fine surfaces such as travertine, and received the AIA Gold Medal in 1971. His imagined talk with a brick ("What do you want, Brick?" "I like an arch.") sums up his respect for materials.

The Richards Medical Research Laboratories in Philadelphia (1960) were a breakthrough, with a clear split between "served" spaces and the "servant" spaces that hold stairs and services. At the Salk Institute in La Jolla (1965), two laboratory wings frame a travertine plaza and a thin channel of water that leads the eye to the Pacific. The Phillips Exeter Academy Library (1971) opens a central atrium through huge circular openings onto the book stacks. The Kimbell Art Museum in Fort Worth (1972) lights its art through slits along the top of cycloid vaults. His last project was the National Assembly of Bangladesh in Dhaka. Louis Kahn's buildings are studied for light, mass and clear construction.

name: Richard Meier
bio:
Richard Meier (born 1934) is an American architect and abstract artist known for geometric buildings in which white dominates. In 1972 he was named one of the New York Five, a group of modernist architects with Peter Eisenman, Michael Graves, Charles Gwathmey and John Hejduk, and in 1984 he won the Pritzker Prize. In 2018 several women accused him of sexual harassment or assault, and he resigned from his firm in 2021.

He first gained wide notice for houses and for The Atheneum, a visitor centre in New Harmony, Indiana (1979), and the High Museum of Art in Atlanta (1983). His design for the Getty Center in Los Angeles (1997), a hilltop complex of concrete and steel clad in travertine or aluminium, raised his profile further; its museum grid is turned 22.5 degrees against the rest of the plan. The Jubilee Church in Rome (2003), meant to recall a ship, rises in three large curved walls of precast concrete, coated in a titanium dioxide cement that breaks down pollution and keeps the walls white. Richard Meier's buildings are studied for their grids, white surfaces and use of daylight.

name: Shigeru Ban
bio:
Shigeru Ban (born 1957) is a Japanese architect known for building with paper, above all recycled cardboard tubes, and for quick, low-cost shelters for people who have lost their homes in disasters. He studied at Cooper Union in New York under John Hejduk, founded the Voluntary Architects' Network in 1995 to build temporary buildings after disasters and conflicts, and won the Pritzker Prize in 2014 for his use of materials and his humanitarian work.

The Paper Dome, a church of paper tubes built in 1995 after the Great Hanshin earthquake, was later rebuilt in Puli, Taiwan. For the Japan Pavilion at Expo 2000 in Hanover, he worked with Frei Otto and the engineers Buro Happold on a 72-metre gridshell of paper tubes. The Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010) is covered by a 90-metre hexagonal roof of laminated timber woven like the cane of a Chinese hat. After the 2011 earthquake in Christchurch, New Zealand, his Cardboard Cathedral (2013) gave the city a transitional church built from more than 90 large cardboard tubes, timber and steel. Shigeru Ban's projects are studied for low-waste materials and for architecture that serves people in crisis.

name: David Chipperfield
bio:
David Chipperfield (born 1953) is a British architect known for restrained museums and public buildings and for careful work with historic ones. Born in London, he worked in the offices of Douglas Stephen, Norman Foster and Richard Rogers before founding David Chipperfield Architects in 1985. He has been knighted for services to architecture and won the Pritzker Prize in 2023.

From 1997 to 2009 he and Julian Harrap rebuilt and restored the Neues Museum in Berlin, largely destroyed in the Second World War. Next to it he added the James Simon Gallery (2019), a gateway to Museum Island whose design draws on the island's building history. The Museum of Modern Literature in Marbach am Neckar (2006) won the Stirling Prize in 2007. In England, The Hepworth Wakefield (2011) is a cluster of ten trapezoid blocks clad in pigmented concrete cast on site, the first of its kind in the UK, with upper galleries lit by large windows in the pitched roofs. Turner Contemporary (2011) stands beside the beach at Margate. David Chipperfield's projects are studied for proportion, material and respect for what is already there.

name: Eero Saarinen
bio:
Eero Saarinen (1910–1961) was a Finnish-American architect and industrial designer known for sweeping concrete shells, arches and cable-hung roofs. The son of the architect Eliel Saarinen, he grew up at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Michigan and studied at Yale. For Knoll he designed furniture such as the Womb chair and the Tulip chair. He died in 1961, aged 51, before several of his best-known buildings were finished.

The Kresge Auditorium at MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts (1955) is a thin concrete shell, one-eighth of a sphere, that touches the ground at only three points. The David S. Ingalls Rink at Yale (1958) hangs its roof on cables from a single concrete backbone, earning the nickname "the whale". The TWA Flight Center in New York (1962) spreads a thin concrete roof like a bird's wings on four Y-shaped piers, and the Washington Dulles Airport Terminal (1962) hangs precast concrete roof panels on cables across the building. The Gateway Arch in St. Louis (1965) is a 192-metre weighted catenary clad in stainless steel and the world's tallest arch. Eero Saarinen's projects are studied for the way structure creates form.

name: Kunio Maekawa
bio:
Kunio Maekawa (1905–1986) was a Japanese architect and a key figure of modernism in post-war Japan. After working in the studios of Le Corbusier and Antonin Raymond, he set up his own firm in 1935 and spent his career holding Japanese tradition and European modernism in tension. Kenzō Tange was among the architects who began in his office, and he received the UIA Auguste Perret Prize in 1963.

His own house of 1942, the House of Kunio Maekawa, now stands at the Edo-Tokyo Open Air Architectural Museum in Koganei. The Tokyo Bunka Kaikan (1961), a concert hall in Ueno Park designed with Junzo Sakakura and Takamasa Yoshizaka, sits beside Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art. His Kyoto Kaikan of 1960 lives on as today's Rohm Theatre Kyoto. From the 1960s he set glazed tiles straight into concrete as it was poured, a method called uchikomi, which became a signature of late works such as the Tokyo Metropolitan Art Museum (1975) and the Museum of East Asian Art in Cologne (1977). Kunio Maekawa's buildings are studied for how modernism can be adapted to local craft.

name: Marcel Breuer
bio:
Marcel Breuer (1902–1981) was a Hungarian-American modernist architect and furniture designer, born in Pécs. One of the first and youngest students at the Bauhaus, he was put in charge of its carpentry workshop and designed the Wassily and Cesca chairs there. In 1937 he followed Walter Gropius to Harvard's Graduate School of Design, and his later buildings, many of them brutalist, made him one of the most popular architects of the mid-20th century.

His first major public commissions came in the 1950s. He designed the UNESCO Headquarters in Paris (1958) with Bernard Zehrfuss and Pier Luigi Nervi, and drew the master plan and church for St. John's Abbey in Collegeville, Minnesota (St. John's Abbey Church, 1961). The Breuer Building in New York (1966), built for the Whitney Museum, steps its granite and concrete floors outward over the entrance like an upside-down ziggurat. The Robert C. Weaver Federal Building in Washington, D.C. (1968), headquarters of the US housing department, has drawn wide criticism; one former housing secretary called it "10 floors of basement". Marcel Breuer's buildings are studied for heavy concrete and stone forms shaped with a furniture maker's eye.

name: Mario Botta
bio:
Mario Botta (born 1943) is a Swiss architect known for buildings made from very simple geometric shapes, often in brick or stone, that create unusual spaces. He designed his first building, a two-family house in Ticino, at 16. He graduated from the Università Iuav di Venezia in 1969, and in Venice he met and worked with Carlo Scarpa, Louis Kahn and Le Corbusier.

Évry Cathedral near Paris (1995) looks as if it were built entirely of brick but is two concrete cylinders faced with brick in horizontal bands. The Church of San Giovanni Battista in Mogno (1996) replaces a 17th-century church flattened by an avalanche in 1986; Botta built it from the marble and granite of the surrounding valleys. The Cymbalista Synagogue in Tel Aviv (1998) raises two matching towers that are square at the base and turn into circles at the top. MART in Rovereto (2002), a "pantheon without a facade", arranges three floors of galleries around a round court under a 40-metre glass dome. Mario Botta's buildings are studied for how symmetry, simple solids and heavy materials give a place its identity.

name: Richard Rogers
bio:
Richard Rogers (1933–2021) was a British and Italian architect, born in Florence, and a leading figure of high-tech architecture. He met Norman Foster while studying at Yale, and in 1963 they set up Team 4 with Su Brumwell and Wendy Cheesman. He was made a life peer, Baron Rogers of Riverside, in 1996, led the British government's Urban Task Force on the decline of cities from 1998, and won the Pritzker Prize in 2007.

With Renzo Piano and Gianfranco Franchini he won the 1971 competition for the Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), the project that made his career. The Lloyd's Building in London (1986), often called the Inside-Out Building, puts its stairs, lifts, ducts and pipes on the outside to leave the floors clear, though the exposed services have made upkeep expensive. The Senedd in Cardiff (2006), home of the Welsh Parliament, uses Welsh slate and oak, a cedar ceiling, and a roof cowl that funnels daylight and air into the chamber below. Madrid-Barajas Airport Terminal 4 (2006) won the Stirling Prize. Richard Rogers's projects are studied for open, flexible floors and for structure and services put on show.

name: Antoni Gaudí
bio:
Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926) was a Catalan architect and designer, the best-known figure of Catalan Modernisme, whose personal style drew on nature, religion and neo-Gothic art. Most of his work is in Barcelona, and between 1984 and 2005 seven of his works were listed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites. He used catenary arches to spread loads evenly, said that no structure was better than a tree trunk or a human skeleton, and covered surfaces in trencadís, a mosaic of broken ceramic.

Palau Güell (1890) was one of several works for his patron, the industrialist Eusebi Güell. Casa Batlló (1906), among his finest buildings, is nicknamed the "House of the Dragon". Casa Milà (1912), called La Pedrera, "the stone quarry", has an undulating, self-supporting stone façade that leaves the floors behind it free to plan. Catenary arches carry both Casa Milà and the Crypt of Colonia Guell (1914). The Sagrada Familia, begun in 1882 under another architect, was less than a quarter built when Gaudí died; with a tower 172.5 metres high, it is now the world's tallest church. Gaudí's buildings are studied for structure learned from nature.

name: BIG
bio:
BIG (Bjarke Ingels Group) is an architecture and design practice founded by the Danish architect Bjarke Ingels in Copenhagen in 2006, after he and Julien De Smedt closed their earlier office, PLOT. It now has offices in cities including New York, London, Barcelona and Shanghai and employs more than 700 people. Its first book and exhibition, Yes Is More, explained its ideas in the form of a comic.

Mountain Dwellings in Copenhagen (2008) climbs apartments up the sloping roof of a car park to make an artificial, south-facing "mountainside". The 8 House (2010) bends a city block into a figure of eight with two courtyards, mixing three kinds of housing with shops and offices. Superkilen (2012), a park in Copenhagen, gathers 108 plants and objects linked to the 62 countries its neighbours come from. Via 57 West in New York (2016), which BIG calls a "courtscraper", rises as a sloping pyramid 142 metres high. CopenHill (2019) puts an 85-metre ski slope, hiking path and climbing wall on top of a waste-to-energy plant. BIG's projects are studied for turning everyday needs, such as parking, housing or power, into public places.

name: Charles Correa
bio:
Charles Correa (1930–2015) was an Indian architect and urban planner based in Mumbai, credited with shaping modern architecture in India after independence. He studied at the University of Michigan and at MIT, and opened his practice in Mumbai in 1958. He was known for concern for the urban poor and his use of traditional methods and materials, and he received the Royal Gold Medal in 1984 and the Praemium Imperiale in 1994.

His first significant project was the Gandhi Smarak Sangrahalaya (1963), the museum at Gandhi's Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad. From 1970 to 1975 he was chief architect for the new city of Navi Mumbai. At the National Crafts Museum in New Delhi (1991) he used what he called "rooms open to the sky", courtyards placed throughout the building. The Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur (1991) takes the nine-square plan of the old city of Jaipur and the Navagraha mandala, each square standing for a planet and the centre left open. Bharat Bhavan, an arts centre in Bhopal (1982), faces the Upper Lake. Charles Correa's projects are studied for courtyards, traditional materials and older ideas of space.

name: Daniel Libeskind
bio:
Daniel Libeskind (born 1946) is a Polish-American architect, artist and teacher, born in Łódź, whose angular, sharply cut buildings are usually placed within deconstructivism. He founded Studio Daniel Libeskind with his wife, Nina, in 1989, and in 2003 he won the competition to draw the master plan for rebuilding the World Trade Center site in New York.

He is best known for the Jewish Museum Berlin (2001), shaped by the history of Jewish life in the city. A line of empty "voids" about 20 metres tall slices through the building, and three axes stand for continuity, emigration and the Holocaust: one leads to the tilted Garden of Exile, another to the Holocaust Tower, an unheated bare concrete silo lit only through a slit in its roof. The Imperial War Museum North in Manchester (2002) is built as three interlocking shards of an imagined globe broken by conflict, standing for air, earth and water. At the Military History Museum in Dresden (2011), a transparent arrowhead cuts through a former arsenal and points towards where the fire-bombing of the city began. Daniel Libeskind's projects are studied for how form can carry memory.

name: Gordon Bunshaft
bio:
Gordon Bunshaft (1909–1990) was an American architect and a leading voice of modern design in the mid-20th century, who spent more than 40 years leading designs at SOM. Born in Buffalo, New York, he studied at MIT and travelled in Europe on a Rotch Travelling Scholarship. He shared the 1988 Pritzker Prize with Oscar Niemeyer and gave the shortest acceptance speech in the prize's history.

Lever House in New York (1952), designed with Natalie de Blois, was in the critic Paul Goldberger's words the city's "first major commercial structure with a glass curtain-wall", after only the United Nations Secretariat. One Chase Manhattan Plaza (28 Liberty Street) (1961) is a 60-storey International Style tower whose plaza holds a sunken rock garden by Isamu Noguchi. The Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library at Yale (1963) has thin marble walls that admit soft light but no direct sun. The Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, D.C. (1974) is an open cylinder raised on four massive piers around a central fountain. Gordon Bunshaft's buildings are studied for clear forms, fine materials and the modern office tower.

name: Henry Hobson Richardson
bio:
Henry Hobson Richardson (1838–1886) was an American architect best known for Richardsonian Romanesque, a highly personal style that adapted the Romanesque architecture of southern France. Born in Louisiana, he studied at Harvard and then, from 1860, at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. With Louis Sullivan and Frank Lloyd Wright he is called one of "the recognized trinity of American architecture", and his Trinity Church in Boston (1872–1877) made his name across the country.

When American architects named the ten best buildings in the country in 1885, half were his, among them Sever Hall at Harvard (1878) and the New York State Capitol in Albany. A series of small public libraries for New England towns defines his style: the Winn Memorial Library in Woburn (1879), the Ames Free Library in Easton (1883) and the Thomas Crane Public Library in Quincy (1881), thought the best of them. The Allegheny County Courthouse in Pittsburgh (1888), one of the two buildings he liked best, was finished after his death by his assistants. Henry Hobson Richardson's buildings are studied for their massing and masonry, and for an American style that influenced Sullivan and Wright.
